name: Ashpile HandStitch Thermal Wrap Layer
description:
A thick, irregular underlayer stitched together from salvaged fleece offcuts, industrial insulation batting, and torn synthetic jersey. Seams are visible and mismatched — some double-stitched with wire thread, others sealed with heat-bond tape. Colors range from ash-gray to oil-stained beige, with dark patches where material sources changed mid-construction. No two are identical.

Common across the Gray Zone settlements near the lake corridor where acid-rain wind cuts through rusted wall gaps at night. Worn under scavenged coats, the bulk shows at the collar and wrists — a clear marker of the Gray Zone survival.
functionality: Provides basic passive insulation against cold and acid-damp. No active systems. Layered construction traps body heat in uneven pockets. Rough inner surface chafes on bare skin — most wearers add a thin cotton slip beneath.
what_it_says: You made this yourself, or someone who cares about you did — survival sewn by hand.
worn_by: children in the Gray Zone family units
manufacturer: Self-made / informal the Gray Zone crafters
story_hooks: A specific stitch pattern identifies this layer as made by a known the Gray Zone seamstress — her work turns up on bodies sometimes, and someone is counting.
Embedded inside the batting: a folded paper with a partial map of a Circuit-level maintenance tunnel entry point.
The heat-bond tape along the left side is partially peeled — underneath is a different fabric entirely, one that doesn't match anything sold in GLMZ.
related_entities: TESSERA CORPONATION Aegis CorpSec Hardened Security BCI

physical_description.visual_profile: Visibly handmade, chunky thermal base layer with an intentionally rough aesthetic. Silhouette is slightly oversized through the torso and shoulders, creating bulk at the neckline and cuffs. The garment reads as DIY salvage—uneven seams catch light, creating a tactile, almost quilt-like appearance. Worn under outerwear, it's meant to show at collar and wrist as a badge of the Gray Zone survival.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and deliberately oversized through the body for maximum insulation and layering capability. Arms are roomy, allowing for thick outerwear over top. Waist is loose, no tailoring. Designed for visibility at edges—collar flares slightly where materials overlap.
physical_description.primary_material: Salvaged fleece offcuts, industrial insulation batting, recycled synthetic jersey in patchwork sections. Heat-bond tape seals at stress points; wire thread visible on reinforced seams.
physical_description.texture: Heavily textured and inconsistent. Fleece sections are soft but napped with use; batting creates quilted, dimpled areas; jersey creates smooth valleys between irregular stitching. Seams are rough, some doubled, creating raised ridgelines. Surface is deliberately imperfect—this is the aesthetic.
physical_description.color_scheme: Mottled ash-gray, oil-stained beige, and dark charcoal where material sources changed mid-construction. No pattern—organic color blocking from salvage scarcity. Oil stains and weathering add unplanned depth.
physical_description.closures: None. Pullover style, meant to be worn as a close underlayer. No fasteners—simple rolled or flat seams at neckline.
distinctive_features: Visible mismatched seams in wire thread and standard thread
Heat-bond tape patches visible on surface
Color shifts mid-construction showing material transitions
Double-stitched reinforcement at shoulders and underarms
Intentional bulk at collar and wrists for visibility when layered
No brand markings—maker's signature is the irregular handwork itself
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 salvage. This is survival wear, not fashion. The construction method and material sourcing scream sub-grade ungoverned zone.
physical_description.cultural_context: the Gray Zone settlement identity. Wearing this announces you survive on salvage, endure acid-rain lake corridor weather, and belong to informal craft communities. It's anti-corpo, anti-sleek—authenticity through imperfection. Also signals technical competence: if you can stitch insulation batting to fleece with wire thread, you know how to survive.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn and weathered from day one. Seams show stress marks; batting is compressed in high-friction areas; oil stains spread naturally over time. The garment doesn't degrade—it ages into its purpose.
